title: JESUS SAID THIS ABOUT MARRIAGE—AND HIS OWN DISCIPLES WONDERED IF IT WAS BETTER NOT TO MARRY
paragraphs: JESUS SAID THIS ABOUT MARRIAGE—AND HIS OWN DISCIPLES WONDERED IF IT WAS BETTER NOT TO MARRY

They had watched Jesus heal the sick, confront demons, forgive sinners, and silence religious leaders. But when He explained what marriage really meant in the eyes of God, even His disciples seemed stunned.
There is a sentence in Matthew 19 that Christians sometimes read too quickly.
We remember Jesus talking about marriage.
We remember the Pharisees asking Him about divorce.
We remember, “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
But then something extraordinary happens.
The disciples hear Jesus.
Not the Pharisees.
Not the hostile crowd.
His own disciples.
Men who had left everything to follow Him.
And their reaction is almost startling:

“If the case of the man be so with his wife, it is not good to marry.”
—Matthew 19:10, KJV
In other words:
If marriage is really that serious… maybe it is better not to get married at all.
Think about that.

Whatever Jesus had just said about marriage was so weighty that His disciples apparently realized marriage was far more serious than simply finding someone you loved, celebrating a wedding, building a home, and hoping everything worked out.
Jesus had taken them somewhere deeper.
Back before the arguments.
Back before the loopholes.
Back before the certificates of divorce.
Back before human beings started asking, “Under what circumstances can I get out?”
Jesus took them back to the beginning.
And maybe that is exactly where some of us need to go.
Because we live in a generation that has become remarkably skilled at discussing relationships while sometimes forgetting the God who created them.
We talk about compatibility.
Chemistry.
Boundaries.
Red flags.
Love languages.
Attraction.
Personal fulfillment.
We ask whether someone “makes us happy.”
And some of those conversations can be useful.
But Jesus asks something deeper.
What did God intend?
The confrontation begins when some Pharisees approach Jesus with a test:

“Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife for every cause?”
—Matthew 19:3, KJV
Matthew tells us they were tempting—or testing—Him.
This was not merely an innocent request for marriage counseling.

Divorce was already the subject of serious Jewish debate. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 was central to those discussions, and different interpretations existed regarding the grounds on which a husband might divorce his wife.
But watch what Jesus does.
They want to begin with divorce.
Jesus begins with creation.

“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female…”
—Matthew 19:4, KJV
Then Jesus brings together the creation language of Genesis:

“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?”
—Matthew 19:5, KJV
And then comes the sentence that still confronts every generation:

“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
—Matthew 19:6, KJV
The Greek is powerful.
Jesus says:
ὃ οὖν ὁ θεὸς συνέζευξεν, ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω
ho oun ho Theos synezeuxen, anthrōpos mē chōrizetō
“What therefore God joined together, let a human being not separate.”
The word translated “joined together,” συνέζευξεν — synezeuxen, carries the idea of joining or yoking together.
Notice who stands at the center of Jesus’ statement.
God.
Not merely the bride.
Not merely the groom.
Not merely the officiant.
God.
That changes the atmosphere of the entire conversation.
Marriage, in Jesus’ teaching, cannot be reduced to a private arrangement between two people that remains meaningful only while both people find it convenient.
Jesus points toward something God Himself established in creation.
And that is why the Pharisees immediately bring up Moses.
If marriage is that serious, they ask, why did Moses command a certificate of divorce?
Jesus answers:

“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”
—Matthew 19:8, KJV
There is a devastating phrase buried inside that answer:
σκληροκαρδία — sklērokardia
Hardness of heart.
The word combines the ideas of hardness and heart.
Suddenly this is not merely a legal discussion.
Jesus has exposed something spiritual.
Sometimes behind the wreckage of human relationships there is something deeper than incompatibility.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Betrayal.
Lust.
Selfishness.
Cruelty.
Refusal to forgive.
Refusal to repent.
A heart becoming harder and harder until someone we once promised to love begins to feel like an enemy.
And before anyone uses this passage as ammunition against someone else, notice where the Gospel always forces us to look eventually:
inside ourselves.
Because hardness of heart is not merely “their” problem.
Every human heart is capable of becoming hard.
You can sing worship songs with a hard heart.
You can quote Scripture with a hard heart.
You can attend church while refusing to apologize.
You can know Christian vocabulary while quietly feeding resentment.
You can appear spiritually mature in public while making your spouse feel invisible at home.
You can win arguments and slowly destroy intimacy.
And sometimes the most frightening words in a marriage are not shouted.
Sometimes they are never spoken.
“I don't care anymore.”
Maybe you know that silence.
Maybe you have slept inches away from someone who felt a thousand miles away.
Maybe you remember when you could not wait to hear their voice.
Now almost every conversation becomes tension.
Maybe you are reading this after betrayal.
Maybe divorce papers have already been signed.
Maybe someone abandoned you despite your desperate attempts to save the marriage.
Maybe abuse shattered what should have been a place of safety.
Maybe you were the one who sinned.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe pornography quietly invaded your marriage.
Maybe anger poisoned your home.
Maybe your spouse begged you to change and you kept saying, “Later.”
Then later finally arrived.
And they were gone.
This is where we must handle Jesus’ words carefully.
The teaching of Matthew 19 should never become a weapon for forcing someone to remain in immediate danger or for pretending that abuse is faithfulness.
Nor should every divorced person be treated as though the circumstances of every broken marriage were identical.

Scripture speaks seriously about marital faithfulness, sexual immorality, abandonment, reconciliation, justice, repentance, and peace. Matthew 19 must therefore be read alongside the broader witness of Scripture, including passages such as Matthew 5:31–32 and 1 Corinthians 7.
Christians have historically differed over some details concerning divorce and remarriage.
But there is something extraordinarily difficult to escape from Jesus’ words:
God takes covenant seriously.
Apparently, the disciples understood exactly how serious He was.
Because after hearing Him, they respond:
“If the case of the man be so with his wife, it is not good to marry.”
Imagine the silence.
Peter looking at John.
John looking at James.
Someone thinking:
Wait.
Marriage means THAT?
Jesus does not respond by lowering the standard.
Instead, He begins speaking about another calling entirely.
Singleness.

“All men cannot receive this saying, save they to whom it is given.”
—Matthew 19:11, KJV
Then Jesus speaks about those who live unmarried lives for different reasons, including those who have chosen celibacy “for the kingdom of heaven’s sake.”
And suddenly another cultural idol falls.
Because Jesus does not teach that marriage is the only path to a meaningful life.
Marriage is sacred.
But marriage is not salvation.
A spouse cannot do what Jesus does.
A wedding ring cannot heal the deepest fracture inside the human soul.
Sex cannot satisfy the eternal hunger for God.
Romance cannot carry the weight of being your god.
And singleness is not a waiting room where incomplete Christians sit until their “real life” begins.
Jesus Christ Himself lived unmarried.
Paul would later speak of singleness as something that could provide unique freedom for devotion to the Lord.
So Scripture refuses both lies.
It refuses the lie that marriage is disposable.
And it refuses the lie that marriage is necessary for human worth.
That means some single person reading this needs to hear something.
You are not half a person.
You are not spiritually defective because you have not married.
Your life does not begin when somebody chooses you.
If you belong to Christ, Someone already has.
And some married person needs to hear something equally uncomfortable.
Your spouse was never meant to be your savior.
You married a sinner.
And your spouse married one too.
That is why Christian marriage cannot survive merely on romance.
Romance is beautiful.
But eventually somebody gets sick.
Somebody loses patience.
Bills arrive.
Bodies change.
Desire fluctuates.
Children exhaust you.
Careers disappoint you.
Parents age.
Temptation appears.
Old wounds surface.
And the person who once seemed almost perfect suddenly becomes painfully human.
Then marriage asks a terrifying question:
Can you love a real person after the fantasy disappears?
The Gospel says something even more shocking.
That is precisely what Christ has done for His people.
He did not love us because we were flawless.
He loved sinners.
Paul writes:
—Romans 5:8, KJV
Jesus did not wait for us to become worthy before moving toward us.
He moved toward rebels.
Toward adulterers.
Toward liars.
Toward hypocrites.
Toward the sexually broken.
Toward the ashamed.
Toward people carrying histories they desperately wished they could erase.
Toward us.
The cross is where holiness and mercy meet without either being compromised.
Jesus does not call evil good.
He does something infinitely better.
He forgives sinners who come to Him.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
This is why a Christian conversation about divorce that contains only rules but no cross has missed the heart of Christianity.
And a Christian conversation about grace that pretends sin does not matter has missed it too.
Jesus gives us neither cheap condemnation nor cheap grace.
He gives us Himself.
Maybe your marriage survived something nobody knows about.
Maybe the photographs on Facebook never showed the nights you cried.
Maybe nobody knows how close everything came to collapsing.
Maybe repentance happened slowly.
Counseling happened painfully.
Trust returned inch by inch.
Prayer became desperate instead of polished.
And somehow, through grace, two wounded people learned to look at each other again.
If that is your story, don't worship your marriage.
Worship the Christ who carried you through it.
And maybe your story ended differently.
Maybe the marriage did collapse.
Maybe you prayed and prayed, and the other person still left.
Maybe you bear responsibility for part of what happened.
Maybe you bear wounds from what someone else chose to do.
Maybe both are true.
And now whenever Christians discuss divorce, something inside you tightens.
Because you are afraid that everybody is looking at you.
Listen carefully.
Your divorce may be part of your story.
It does not have to become your identity.
Your failure does not have to receive the final sentence.
Neither does what somebody else did to you.
The woman at the well had a complicated relational history.
Jesus knew it.
He did not flatter her.
He did not hide the truth.
But He also did not walk away.
He offered living water.
That is Jesus.
Truth without cruelty.
Grace without pretending.
Holiness without hypocrisy.
Mercy without denying sin.
Perhaps that is why some of us find Matthew 19 uncomfortable.
We want Jesus to take our side.
Instead, He calls us to surrender.
The Pharisees came asking for the boundaries of permissible divorce.
Jesus exposed the hardness of the human heart.
The disciples responded by wondering whether marriage was worth the risk.
Jesus pointed beyond both marriage and singleness toward the kingdom of heaven.
And eventually every path leads us to the same question:
Who is Lord?
Not:
“Can I justify myself?”
Not:
“Can I prove my ex was worse?”
Not:
“Can I find a loophole?”
Not:
“Can I hide what I did?”
Who is Lord?
Because Christianity is not ultimately about repairing your public image.
It is about surrendering your life to Jesus Christ.
Maybe you need to repent today.
Not your spouse.
Not your ex.
You.
Maybe the sentence you have been waiting for God to tell somebody else is the sentence He is speaking to you.
Apologize.
Confess.
Stop hiding.
Get help.
End the affair.
Put away the secret messages.
Stop feeding pornography.
Stop weaponizing silence.
Stop humiliating your spouse.
Stop pretending cruelty is “leadership.”
Stop using Scripture to control somebody.
Stop making excuses for what God is calling you to surrender.
Come into the light.
And if you have sinned so badly that you think God could never want you again, look at the cross before you finish that sentence.
Peter denied Jesus.
The thief beside Christ was dying under the consequences of his crimes.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The Gospel was never a trophy for people with spotless histories.
It is good news for sinners.
Repentance does not mean pretending the consequences disappear.
Some relationships cannot simply return to what they were.
Trust may require time.
Reconciliation requires more than words and cannot always be achieved by one person alone.
Forgiveness does not require pretending abuse never occurred.
Grace does not erase wisdom, accountability, justice, or appropriate boundaries.
But repentance means you stop running from God.
You turn.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια — metanoia.
Repentance.
A turning of mind and life toward God.
And maybe someone reading this has been running for years.
You know Christian language.
You know how to smile in church.
You know how to post Bible verses.
But when the room gets quiet, you know there is something between you and God that you keep refusing to surrender.
No more hiding.
Jesus already knows.
And somehow…
He is still calling you.
That is the scandal.
And that is the grace.
The scandal is that sinners like us have rebelled against a holy God.
The grace is that the Son of God stepped into our wreckage.
He carried sin to Calvary.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Not so we could become better actors.
So we could become new creations.
Maybe your marriage needs resurrection.
Maybe your heart does.
Maybe your first prayer after reading this should not be, “Lord, change them.”
Maybe it should be:
“Jesus, search me.”
You do not have to tell strangers every detail.
But sometimes bringing even a few honest words into the light becomes the first crack in the wall we spent years building around ourselves.
Then look around the comments.
You may discover you were never the only one bleeding.
Let them encounter Jesus here.
Because someday emotion may get loud and truth may suddenly feel difficult to remember.
Come back.
Read Matthew 19 again.
Read Genesis 2.
Read 1 Corinthians 7.
Read Ephesians 5.
And above everything else, keep looking at Jesus.
Biblical generosity must never be manipulated.
But voluntary financial support can become one practical expression of generosity toward Gospel work you believe is bearing fruit.
But whether you ever give a cent or not, do something far more important.
Follow Jesus.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Jesus.
Because perhaps someone you know is one article away from finally admitting:
“My marriage needs help.”
“My heart has become hard.”
“I need to repent.”
“I need forgiveness.”
“I need Jesus.”
Matthew 19 begins with religious men asking Jesus about divorce.
But beneath their question is a problem far older than divorce.
The human heart.
And that is why our greatest hope is not merely finding the perfect spouse.
It is not remaining single.
It is not winning the argument.
It is not maintaining the appearance of a perfect Christian family.
Our hope is Christ.
The One who can take a heart made hard by years of sin and teach it to feel again.
The One who can take shame and replace it with mercy.
The One who can confront sin without abandoning the sinner who repents.
The One who can enter stories filled with betrayal, regret, loneliness, broken promises, divorce papers, tears, consequences, repentance, forgiveness, and scars…
and still write something beautiful.
So perhaps the disciples were right to tremble when they understood how serious marriage really was.
But there is an even greater truth worth trembling over.
The God who takes covenant seriously is also the God whose mercy can reach people after they have seriously failed.
And when everyone else thinks your worst chapter deserves to become your ending…
Jesus may only be reaching for the pen.
